title: 'I paid thousands to a company for jobs that never came'
content: A company has been accused of promising jobs in the healthcare sector which never materialised, leaving people thousands of pounds out of pocket. Registered in 2025, Synetal Solutions Ltd says it offers career-focused training programmes in the healthcare and IT sectors. But the BBC has spoken to a number of people who claim they were promised training and support to secure sponsored healthcare jobs that never became available to apply for. London Citizens Advice says it has seen an increase in recruitment-related scams since the government stopped overseas recruitment for care workers . The charity described the firm's practices as "unethical". Synetal Solutions says it "takes these concerns seriously and disputes the broad allegation that its services or candidate outcomes are fictitious". Apurv Patel, who has been in the UK on a Skilled Worker visa since 2023, said he paid Synetal Solutions £3,600 across February and March for healthcare training after he and a friend were verbally promised guaranteed sponsored jobs. Eight months later he has received no job offers, interviews or meaningful employment support, he said. "I'm frustrated. I paid money, I wasted my time. I did whatever they wanted without any result," he said. "It's had a miserable effect on my family and finances." Patel said he did receive some training but described it as poor quality and ultimately "worthless". Having previously worked for two years as a healthcare assistant, he said he became concerned when a trainer was unable to answer routine questions about care work. "She didn't give us any answers and we realised she didn't have any experience of healthcare," he said. The company disputes claims that training was ineffective. He also alleged communication with the company deteriorated after he made his second payment, with responses sometimes taking several days. Patel has since complained to his bank and sought help from Citizens Advice. The BBC has seen emails from the company advertising a "three-month recruitment programme" offering "training and placement with sponsorship" for £5,500. Home Office guidance states agencies may charge for services such as training or CV-writing assistance, but cannot charge fees solely for finding, or attempting to find, employment. Responding to questions about its marketing, Synetal Solutions said: "We acknowledge the 'guarantee' wording in the emails supplied and recognise that contractual terms alone do not resolve concerns about those assurances." As part of its programme, Synetal Solutions created accounts for trainees on iHasco, a health and social care training platform. The BBC contacted iHasco, which confirmed the company was a customer. However, it said its terms did not permit customers to resell its training content to individuals who were not employees. The company said it was reviewing Synetal Solutions' account and would take appropriate action if necessary. Synetal Solutions said it had acted in accordance with its agreement with iHasco. The Care Quality Commission said there was no single qualification that automatically qualified someone to work as a care worker. Instead, providers are responsible for ensuring employees are appropriately trained and competent for their roles. The BBC also contacted a number of healthcare organisations whose logos appeared on Synetal Solutions' website as examples of employers where graduates had worked. Those organisations that responded said they had no links to the company. Some also said they had not authorised the use of their branding, and some said they would not accept certificates provided through the company's training. Daniel Blake, director of London Citizens Advice, described the company's approach as "exploitative". "The promises that were made are impossible promises," he said. "They are targeting people with vulnerable immigration status. "This company is asking for large sums of money upfront without any reputable standards, without any reputable evidence of success, and yet when it goes wrong they are refusing to take any responsibility. "For us, it seems a very unethical way of conducting business." He added that no reputable recruitment agency would guarantee a successful outcome without first assessing a candidate and matching them to a suitable role, and urged anybody asked to pay large sums upfront to seek independent advice. "If it seems too good to be true, it probably is," he said. The company's website stated: "Synetal Solutions provides the right support, guidance, and guaranteed job placement to help you succeed." But since the BBC contacted Synetal Solutions mentions of job guarantees were removed from the website. Its social media channels also promoted healthcare as "one of the most reliable paths" for people seeking visa-sponsored work in the UK. Sarah and Rahul, whose names we have changed, said they paid £3,000 to Synetal Solutions while seeking sponsored employment before the expiry of their student visas. Rahul, a former dentist in India, could remain in the UK on a graduate visa for longer, but Sarah's immigration status was close to expiring. To pay the fee, the couple said they borrowed money from a family friend and took out a loan. Rahul said he was shocked by the quality of the training. "The mentor didn't know anything about healthcare," he said. The couple said they were also shown the names of established healthcare providers, including Bupa, as examples of potential employers. Bupa told the BBC it had no connection with the company. Synetal Solutions says some of their candidates "told us they had secured employment with Bupa" and the reference was "not intended to suggest a formal partnership with Bupa". It says it had not verified those outcomes and "cannot attribute the recruitment decisions to our training". Rahul said he secured one or two interviews, but prospective employers rejected the certificates he had received through the programme. The couple said Synetal Solutions had since stopped responding to their messages. "We're desperate," Sarah said. "We don't see any other way out." Amisha, whose name has also been changed, said she signed up with Synetal after being told that both a placement and visa sponsorship were guaranteed. Her student visa is due to expire soon. She said the training consisted of three sessions lasting around 90 minutes each. After paying an initial instalment of £1,800, she became reluctant to make a second payment because she felt she had received little in return. She said the company warned her that her contract would be cancelled if she failed to pay, prompting her to transfer a further £1,800. "I was waiting for interviews for two or three months. They were ignoring me," she said. According to Amisha, the company applied for only a handful of vacancies advertised on job-search website Indeed. She eventually secured an interview for a healthcare assistant role, but said the employer told her the certificates she had received were not recognised. The BBC also identified what appeared to be at least a couple of stock photographs or AI-generated images used as testimonials on the company's website. The company said it had not authenticated the two reviews identified, and removed them after we contacted them. Teni Shahiean, an immigration lawyer at OTS Solicitors, said it was "particularly concerning" where individuals facing visa deadlines were being asked to make substantial payments on the understanding that jobs, sponsorship or immigration outcomes were seemingly guaranteed. She urged caution, adding that a job offer alone does not guarantee someone will be able to remain in the UK. "The outcome can depend on the role, the sponsor, the individual meeting the relevant immigration requirements and, ultimately, any decision by the Home Office," she said. Blake told the BBC: "If it seems good to be true, it probably is. If you are considering handing over money upfront then seek advice." He said that "if people have given money and haven't received the service that they were entitled to they should seek redress". "First of all, make a complaint directly to the company, then to Trading Standards. "If people feel a criminal offence has happened, we would encourage and support them to go to the police." A government spokesperson said: "We know how much distress scammers cause to their victims, which is why we will do everything in our power to protect hardworking families and vulnerable customers. "Our reforms have provided Companies House with new and improved powers to prevent companies from acting unlawfully and to query, remove and share suspicious information." Synetal Solutions said: "We provide training and employment assistance and maintain supporting records. Recruitment, sponsorship and visa decisions depend on employers and the Home Office." The company said it had records of genuine candidates who had secured jobs and sponsorship through its services. After Primark announced plans for home delivery, we hear from women who never go into clothes stores. Women with endometriosis are suffering financially as well as physically, a new report by MPs warns. The fire service says the changes will apply to its wholetime firefighters' recruitment process. The cuts equate to around 6% of the streaming giant's total workforce worldwide. The Competition and Markets Authority has fined Wayfair, Appliances Direct, and Gold's Gym £6m in total. title: I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online
content: Jess Bacon does all her clothes shopping online. As a plus-size woman, she finds the size ranges available in stores unreliable. "The sizing in store is notoriously bad. I find it quite demoralising in store," she says. "The average size woman in the UK is a size 14 or a size 16. I think a lot of people just don't feel seen or represented," says the 29-year-old from Peterborough. Jess, a culture journalist and author, finds shopping online "much quicker than going into a store, paying for parking, trying things on". And she feels posting back items that don't fit is less hassle than returning in store, while frequent visits to her local post office give her "more of a community connection". Jess notes Primark is one of the few High Street retailers where plus-size people can shop. In her experience, Primark stores usually stock up to a size 22. But soon she'll have the option of staying home even for this - as, after years of holding out, Primark now plans to launch a home delivery service in Britain . Even throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, when shops were closed, Primark didn't offer the ability to shop online. In 2022 it launched a click-and-collect service, but shoppers still had to travel for their purchases. The retailer has not said when it expects to launch the service, but has bought a warehouse in Sheffield to enable it to ship products to homes. Analysts say the decision shows Primark is facing major challenges from ultra-fast-fashion brands such as Shein. Online shopping had been on the rise even before the surge seen during the pandemic. Online accounted for 27.3% of all retail sales in August this year, according to the Office for National Statistics, up from 18.1% in August 2019. Internet shopping has also been boosted by the decline of the High Street in many parts of the country, something which Jess has noticed in Peterborough. "We don't have John Lewis [anymore]. There's kind of not that much of a reason to go into town." Like Jess, Julia Mitchell, who lives near Chichester, doesn't enjoy in-person clothes shopping. She finds it overstimulating and thinks there are better bargains to be had online. "I basically never go into them [clothes shops]. It's not really something I enjoy," the 32-year-old says. "I guess some people might be able to see stuff and pick it up and look at it, but for me, being able to get the best price is more important." Julia, a content creator, tries to shop ethically and most of her purchases are second hand from Vinted. The one thing she never shops online for, though, is books. "The thing about bookshops is that they are cultural spaces and community spaces." Sandra Davies does all her shopping online. She has had three strokes and finds walking to and around stores too much physically. "I've tried it on two occasions but on both times, standing in a queue for over 10 minutes was too much for me and I collapsed." The 61-year-old from Sheffield says waiting for deliveries can be taxing as well, as she worries about missing the postie and having to reschedule. Julie Palmer, a retail analyst, is not surprised that Primark has finally moved into home deliveries as it has evidently recognised that "online sales bring scale". However, she says a shop's returns policy for online purchases can "make or break" it. Many brands offer hassle-free returns, which Palmer says Primark must match in order to compete. "Shoppers want them to be free, simple and quick. That means a generous window, lots of drop-off options and refunds that land within days, not weeks. "When a policy is clunky or slow, customers remember it and shop elsewhere next time." But returns are expensive for retailers. Some, like Asos, have started charging a fee if customers make frequent returns. This is a balancing act, Palmer says, "because a fee can easily push a customer to a competitor". "Most retailers that charge still offer free returns in store, which is a deliberate way to get people through the door and hopefully spending again." Apurv Patel is one of several people who say they were promised job opportunities that did not appear. The cuts equate to around 6% of the streaming giant's total workforce worldwide. title: Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm
content: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has said she is "minded to intervene" in the proposed £1.6bn deal for Sky to buy ITV's media and entertainment division. Nandy said there were reasonable grounds to believe the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape. Sky said it would "carefully consider" a letter from the culture secretary and "engage constructively" with the review into the deal. "We remain confident that bringing Sky and ITV's media and entertainment business together will create a stronger British media," it said. ITV welcomed the letter and said the deal would help it "compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries". The two companies announced in July that Sky had agreed to buy ITV's broadcasting business, including its free-to-air TV channels and the ITV X streaming service. The deal does not include ITV's production arm, ITV Studios, which makes popular programmes such as Love Island and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here. It would give Sky access to millions more viewers, while bosses hope it would help both compete with streaming giants such as Netflix. But Nandy has told Sky and ITV that she is considering issuing a public interest intervention notice (PIIN) to the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) and regulator Ofcom, forcing an investigation into the tie-up. In a letter to both companies, she said she was minded to order the probe to address public interest considerations including: The letter said Nandy recognised Sky News and ITV News were two of the most prominent sources of television news in the UK, with a joint 26% share of those viewing news on linear TV. Consumers would still have access to other sources of news such as the BBC and Channel 4, it added. But Nandy believes that, over time, the tie-up could undermine the range of views available to viewers, with 86% of the linear TV news market controlled by the BBC and Sky/ITV. The North of England could be particularly hard hit as well as nations of the UK other than England and those from lower socio-economic backgrounds, the letter argued. This is because their main source of news is broadcast news, it added. Sky and ITV have been given until 20 October to respond to the culture secretary's concerns. A Sky spokesperson said: "We have already made clear commitments to protect ITV's identity, its free-to-air services and public service broadcasting obligations, and to ensure ITV News and Sky News remain distinct editorial voices." An ITV spokesperson said: "We welcome the publication of the secretary of state's 'minded to' issue a public interest intervention notice letter as was expected and look forward to fully co-operating in the process. "This is another important milestone in the regulatory review process towards creating a UK player with the scale and resources to better compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries." Nandy's intervention would be made under a new public interest consideration. This would need legislation to be brought forward, given that current laws do not cover the effect of a merger on streaming or on-demand programmes. She said: "If I decide to intervene on the basis of this new public interest consideration, I will bring forward legislation... to extend the application of the public interest consideration relating to the availability of a wide range of broadcasting to on-demand programmes."
